title: Indonesia raises rates to defend the rupiah while keeping credit incentives in place
summary: Bank Indonesia raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.00% at its 17–18 November meeting. It also lifted the deposit and lending facility rates by 25 basis points to 5.25% and 6.75%. October inflation had edged lower, and the Board still expected it to stay within the 1.5–3.5% target range in 2026 and 2027. The hike was pre-emptive. The Bank judged that stabilising the rupiah as global financial conditions tightened would help protect the inflation outlook. At the same time it strengthened incentives for banks to lend to the real economy.

The release’s external-sector figures explain why a trade surplus and aggregate capital inflows had offered incomplete protection. By 17 November the rupiah had weakened 0.66% from end-October, to 18,245 per US dollar. In the fourth quarter through 16 November, equities had seen USD 0.9 billion of outflows, while overall capital flows showed USD 4.80 billion of net inflows. Government issues of global bonds and sukuk, together with flows into government securities, accounted for much of the support. Those transactions have different timing and investors from a purchase of local equities. Their inclusion in the aggregate makes it difficult to infer broad foreign appetite for Indonesian assets. The Bank’s view that the currency would remain stable depended in part on maintaining attractive rupiah yields.

Bank Indonesia linked a strong dollar to global portfolio reallocation. Its international outlook envisaged further US monetary tightening, elevated Treasury yields and reduced emerging-market exposure amid geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over AI equity valuations. In Indonesia, annual inflation eased from 3.28% to 3.23% in October. Core inflation declined to 2.56%, while weather-related production losses helped lift volatile food inflation to 5.81%. A rate increase can affect the local-currency cost of imports. It cannot quickly restore a weather-damaged harvest. The Bank paired exchange-rate stabilisation with government food-supply measures.

The numbered policy measures show how the Bank intended to support demand for rupiah assets while protecting access to funding. It retained offshore forward and domestic spot and forward intervention. For hedges arranged via partner banks it increased the premium discount on six-month domestic non-deliverable forwards from 40% to 45%, and on twelve-month forwards from 45% to 50%. The discounts change the cost of hedging for eligible users. They do not tell an investor the resulting all-in return or the amount of new foreign demand. A planned cross-currency repo facility, effective by March 2027, would allow banks to borrow rupiah against specified foreign-currency Bank Indonesia securities.

Domestic activity gave the Board some room to raise rates. Annual GDP growth reached 5.47% in the third quarter, up from 5.29% in the second, with consumption and investment supporting the expansion. Loan growth was 13.21% in October, but investment lending grew 21.32% and consumer loans just 4.73%. From 1 December a financing incentive of up to 3% of third-party funds would support lending to job-creating sectors and small businesses. A separate incentive of up to 2% aimed to improve liquidity distribution through money markets. The amounts available to banks measure incentives, not additional loans. Whether they offset tighter funding for the intended borrowers was still an open question.

The closing bank and payments data supplied context for that choice. September’s system capital ratio was 24.30% and gross non-performing loans were 2.07%, while the Bank continued expanding digital payment acceptance and oversight. These aggregate readings supported its assessment of resilience. They gave no borrower-level evidence that a higher policy rate could be absorbed equally well by companies, consumers and small firms.

questions.question: How much of the external support was recurring demand for rupiah assets?
questions.detail: The Bank reports net capital inflows despite equity outflows and a weaker currency. Separate sovereign global issuance and local government bond flows from foreign purchases of equities, then align settlement dates with the currency moves. Bank Indonesia’s balance-of-payments and securities statistics and the government’s issuance notices would help test how much support might persist between borrowing operations. That distinction matters to the expected protection from holding local-currency debt.

questions.question: Did larger hedging discounts improve the return available after hedging?
questions.detail: The announced changes apply at specific tenors and through partner banks. Compare executable six- and twelve-month domestic forward prices, eligibility and fees with offshore quotes around the decision. Use official operation results to distinguish turnover from new positions and look for evidence of shifts between hedging venues. Without those details, the premium discounts and past transaction volume cannot establish a profitable carry trade or a durable increase in inflows.

questions.question: Could the liquidity incentives reach the borrowers most exposed to the higher rate?
questions.detail: Investment and consumer lending were already growing at very different speeds. Compare deposit repricing, funding costs and new loan rates across banks with different use of the financing and money-market incentives. Official lending statistics and bank disclosures by borrower size could distinguish new credit from refinancing. That would help assess whether higher policy rates mainly defend the currency or also materially reduce household and small-business spending.
